codex.worst_flaw: The safety audit samples only credited jobs, leaving the pilot without a way to detect skipped checks or unreported hazards on jobs that earn no credit.

claude.worst_flaw: The audit samples only ten credited jobs a week with no planned check for displacement (for example, technicians skipping or delaying the logging of hazards, or uncredited jobs and fallback use rising in reward crews), and it has no independent shadow validation or staffed appeal beyond a single steward, so gaming and miscounts could go undetected at 300-person scale.

holistic.reason: Co-designed with stewards, fixes friction before rewards, pays for safety holds equally, and has audits and a pause trigger, though the modest team-meal reward and heavy measurement/process complexity limit salience and some durability.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the safety audit can independently detect unreported hazards and verify actual job-start times, because both can affect whether crews earn paid time.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew-level 55% threshold with shared reward lets peers pressure low-volume or hazard-flagging technicians, and the five-job weekly sample across 300 technicians is too thin to catch rushed or backfilled checklists before rewards settle, with no independent shadow validation or versioned event log to back corrections and appeals.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, union-friendly pilot with fair crew-wide reward, friction fixes, a staggered control, and quality safeguards, but a 30-minute reward is modest, the 55% threshold is only moderately above the 35% baseline, and durability depends on whether the app fixes stick once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: Checklist quality is checked only through a small weekly sample of 8 records with no independent field observation, so tick-through completion could inflate the headline metric without materially changing pre-job hazard assessment; appeals and corrections also rest on one coordinator with no versioned event history or independent shadow validation.

codex.worst_flaw: Reward launch should wait for independent verification that technicians actually perform the safety checks, since a rushed or false submission can still agree with the dispatch and safety records used in the audit.

holistic.reason: Workflow-first fixes, union co-design, team-level paid time, private progress, randomized staggered rollout and quality sampling with a pause rule are strong and union-friendly, but the 75% threshold only sees the reward in a four-week window, the reward is modest and low-salience, and the measurement dependency on job-start records, and the one-coordinator sampling load, are real risks.

claude.worst_flaw: The 85% target is not tied to a feasibility check, and it is all-or-nothing over four weeks. It also does not adjust for PR size or complexity, so with only two groups and five-review quality samples, a miss or an apparent effect is hard to interpret.

codex.worst_flaw: The shared reward hinges on an 85% cutoff with no minimum PR count or adjustment for review complexity, so a single difficult PR can decide whether a low-volume group earns it.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with fair measurement, anti-gaming checks, a non-cash team reward and a clear drop/keep rule, but it is complex to run, the reward is modest, and lasting change depends on the workflow fixes rather than the incentive.

codex.worst_flaw: If the team shares one queue, the pilot cannot reliably distinguish the lunch reward’s effect from the effects of the workflow fixes or changes in PR volume and complexity.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group when the team shares one review queue, and the 80% keep threshold is not tied to the reconstructed baseline or to sample size. That leaves the gain from the lunch over the workflow fixes unmeasured, and with 25 engineers the weekly percentages will be noisy.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck (queue, protected time, backup), uses a small team-level reward with quality checks and a clear keep/change/drop rule, but a lunch is a weak hook for sceptical engineers and the 8-hour window may feel tight.

claude.worst_flaw: The two-group stagger, with only two ownership groups and no stated uncertainty or sample-size reasoning, can't credibly isolate the reward's added value, and the team-wide 80% keep threshold isn't checked against a comparison or against the queue fixes alone.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-group stagger leaves differences in PR complexity, reviewer capacity, and spillover unaccounted for, so it cannot reliably isolate the reward’s effect from the shared workflow changes.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, protecting review time, using clear clock rules, quality sampling and a staggered comparison suits sceptical engineers, but the modest team lunch reward may barely register and the 45-minute weekly overhead and manual sampling may not hold up.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot support a decision to roll out the kiosk because it never measures what share of eligible hand-hygiene moments nurses actually log.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no staffed appeal route, no versioned audit or policy record and no independent check of Infection Prevention's ward rates, so a disputed reward decision cannot be traced or contested. The reward is also tied to observed audits, which can capture behaviour that changes when observers are present.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with audited outcomes, safeguards, and a staggered rollout, but ward-pooled rewards weaken individual motivation, the modest meal reward is low-salience, and behaviour likely fades once rewards stop.

codex.worst_flaw: The keep-or-drop decision relies on an unvalidated recall survey that excludes nurses who cannot remember and never checks reported logging against eligible opportunities.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward depends on monthly audits that staff know are coming, and the design admits observer effects (people behave differently when watched) without fixing them: there are no unannounced or covert audit checks, no displacement checks between audited and unaudited shifts, and no staffed appeal or replayable audit record. The core reward measure is therefore open to inflation from observation effects.

holistic.reason: Rigorous, safe design that ties the reward to audited care, but the reward is a modest meal, the audit-based target may feel remote from daily kiosk use, and the sustained 'default kiosk' plan is untested.

claude.worst_flaw: The design says it wants nurses logging in the kiosk, but it pays only on monthly observer audits and never defines what a logged moment is or ties it to real opportunities, so whether the kiosk is worth using is never measured or tested, and auditing, appeals and data versioning are left thin.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot determine how often nurses log eligible hand-hygiene moments or whether those logs help wards solve workflow problems, so it lacks a sound basis for keeping the kiosk.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with audit-based rewards, staggered randomisation, safety stops and workflow fixes, but a once-off ward meal is a weak motivator, three wards limits inference, and durability depends on the kiosk actually helping nurses rather than adding work.

codex.worst_flaw: The 50% reward threshold counts tickets for which linking is inappropriate and ignores queue case mix, so teams with fewer genuine opportunities can lose the reward or feel pressure to add irrelevant links.

claude.worst_flaw: Every agent gets the same target of one contribution per two tickets, with no adjustment for queue, case mix or small ticket counts, and the existing CSAT bonus may still push agents to avoid hard cases or link generic articles.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with fixed denominators, sampling audits, CSAT guardrails, randomized staggered rollout and workflow fixes, though a team-level meal reward and a 50% target from 12% are ambitious and the lasting effect depends mostly on the workflow change sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The staggered pilot leaves team assignment and the timing of workflow changes uncontrolled, making it hard to isolate the reward’s effect on article coverage.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot keeps the CSAT bonus and tracks CSAT only as a lagging team-level trigger. It never checks whether linking articles helps resolution quality, and 10 sampled tickets a week is too few to catch irrelevant links across 60 agents.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with a count-once rule, private feedback, a staggered comparison, quality sampling and CSAT guardrails, but the 30-minute team reward is modest, a 30% target from 12% is ambitious, and durability relies on the workflow default and suggested links, not on lasting motivation.

codex.worst_flaw: The same reward threshold applies even when queues differ in how often agents can safely attach a useful article, so ticket mix can determine which teams earn the meal.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never reconciles the article goal with the existing CSAT bonus and only watches CSAT at team level, and it gives no event history, appeal path or staffing for disputed credit, so contested counts and any trade-off between CSAT and articles go unresolved.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, a quality gate, randomized rollout and safeguards against gaming and CSAT harm, but a 35% target from 12% in four weeks with a team meal is a modest incentive, and noticing depends on the weekly channel post, so durability rests mainly on the workflow fixes.
